message.content: Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) diverge at the level of the two major clades of placental mammals that give rise to modern carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates. Their most recent common ancestor was a **Laurasiatherian placental mammal** that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago during the late Cretaceous/early Paleocene. This ancestor would have been a small, generalized mammal that eventually split into the lineages leading to the perissodactyls (which include horses, rhinos, and zebras) and the carnivorans (which include cats, dogs, bears, etc.).
message.reasoning: The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want an answer. There's no tool needed. Just respond with a concise answer. Probably mention that lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) share a common ancestor in the order Carnivora? Actually lions are Felidae, family within order Carnivora. Zebras are Equidae, also order Perissodactyla. Wait, zebras are odd-toed ungulates, order Perissodactyla. Lions are even-toed ungulate? No, lions are mammals but not ungulates. They belong to order Carnivora. So their common ancestor would be at the level of class Mammalia. But maybe they share a more recent common ancestor at the level of clade Eutheria (placental mammals). So answer: The most recent common ancestor of lions and zebras is a placental mammal from the clade Laurasiatheria, likely a member of the group that gave rise to both perissodactyls and carnivorans. That ancestor lived around 70 million years ago. So answer accordingly.
